paras: The reported shooting of two men at San Marcial was a killing, said to have happened in New Mexico Territory in about January 1881, in which townspeople were reported to have shot two "desperadoes" to death in a saloon. The only account came from a traveler interviewed by the Leadville Herald, and it was reprinted in papers across the country as a frontier curiosity. A New Mexico paper, the Las Vegas Morning Gazette, said no one there knew of the affair and gave the story no credence.

According to a Leadville telegram, the Herald interviewed a former Leadville resident just back from Colorado, N. Mex., then the end of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe line. He said three men had been lynched there for robbing a woman, Mary McBride, and that he went on to San Marcial the next day.

By the traveler's account, he had just sat down at his hotel table in San Marcial when shrieks and revolver fire drew the guests outside, where two riders were shooting in the dark. The whole town was said to have taken up arms and chased the pair to the old town of San Marcial, where they rode into a saloon, shot out the lights and took over the bar.

Citizens from the new town then surrounded the saloon in silence, and once the proprietor had left, "the entire party" fired volley after volley into it. A later examination was said to have found seventy-one balls in the two bodies, and the next day the dead men were thrown into a hole dug in the prairie. No report names the two men or gives their race.
The coverage contains no report of an inquest, arrests or official notice of the killings.

The story moved east as a Leadville telegram, appearing in the Chicago Daily Tribune on January 19, 1881, under "Far-West Episodes," and, according to the Las Vegas Gazette, on the front page of the St. Louis Globe-Democrat under "Lawlessness Quickly Quelled by the Masses." Southern papers reprinted the full Herald text under headlines such as "How They Dispose of Roughs in San Marcial" and "No Unnecessary Ceremony Over It," printing it without comment. A news-items brief in papers in Mississippi, Tennessee and Louisiana shortened it to one sentence, saying the two desperadoes were "disposed of in an equally summary manner."
The Las Vegas Morning Gazette took a different line, heading its reprint "A Horrible Yarn" and complaining that New Mexico's reputation in the states made the public "easily gulled" by such stories.
Whether the shooting happened is unsettled, since every printing goes back to one anonymous interview, while the Gazette rejected it only because no one in Las Vegas had heard of it.

bases: The only account describes townspeople pursuing two men and shooting them to death in a saloon without any legal process [A1, A6]; the victims' race is never stated.

As told, citizens from the new town acting as a party killed two 'desperadoes' for terrorizing the town, which would meet the definition [A1, A6]. But the story comes only from an unnamed traveler's second-hand interview, with no names or date, and the Las Vegas Gazette said no one in New Mexico knew of it and gave it no credence [A2], so whether any killing took place is unestablished.
Every report traces to one Leadville Herald interview [A1, A3, A6], and the one New Mexico paper in the coverage rejected it as a 'yarn' [A2].

A news-items brief reduced it to one sentence pairing it with the Colorado, N. Mex., lynching: two desperadoes 'disposed of in an equally summary manner'.
The Las Vegas Morning Gazette headed it 'A Horrible Yarn' and disbelieved it, defending the territory rather than commenting on the killing itself.
